body:
**Savings rate and time.** These matter more than return. The table below is my own illustration. It assumes a monthly SIP with returns compounded monthly. The 12% row is a plausible long-run diversified-equity assumption, not a promise. 15% is what a genuinely skilled investor might sustain. 18% for 30 years is a record almost nobody achieves: Lynch did 29% for only 13 years, and Buffett's partnership 23.8% for 13.

| Monthly SIP | Years | Invested | At 8% | At 12% | At 15% | At 18% |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| ₹10,000 | 10 | ₹12 lakh | ₹18 lakh | ₹22 lakh | ₹26 lakh | ₹31 lakh |
| ₹10,000 | 20 | ₹24 lakh | ₹57 lakh | ₹92 lakh | ₹1.33 cr | ₹1.93 cr |
| ₹10,000 | 30 | ₹36 lakh | ₹1.42 cr | ₹3.08 cr | ₹5.63 cr | ₹10.4 cr |
| ₹25,000 | 20 | ₹60 lakh | ₹1.43 cr | ₹2.30 cr | ₹3.32 cr | ₹4.82 cr |
| ₹25,000 | 30 | ₹90 lakh | ₹3.54 cr | ₹7.70 cr | ₹14.1 cr | ₹26.0 cr |
| ₹50,000 | 30 | ₹1.8 cr | ₹7.09 cr | ₹15.4 cr | ₹28.2 cr | ₹52.0 cr |
| ₹25,000, raised 10% a year | 30 | — | ₹11.6 cr | ₹20.0 cr | ₹31.6 cr | — |

Four lessons follow from the table. First, saving ₹25,000 a month at an ordinary 12% (₹7.7 crore) beats saving ₹10,000 a month at an elite 15% (₹5.6 crore). Your savings rate is a lever you control completely, and alpha is not. Second, raising your SIP 10% a year with your salary nearly triples the outcome, which is worth more than any stock tip. Third, the years from 20 to 30 do most of the work, so starting a decade late costs more than picking badly. Fourth, inflation is real. At 6% a year, ₹1 crore thirty years from now buys roughly what ₹17 lakh buys today, so ₹7.7 crore nominal is a comfortable retirement, not a Forbes listing. A one-time ₹10 lakh at 30% a year for ten years becomes about ₹1.4 crore. That is roughly what an outlier like Porinju's best stretch could deliver, and it is still not generational wealth.

**What to stop doing.** Stop trading weekly and expiry-day options, buying or selling. Stop paying for Telegram, WhatsApp or "course" calls from unregistered advisers: SEBI's orders against Sundar, "Baap of Chart" and Avadhut Sathe show the reliable money flows from followers to the influencer. Stop copying bulk deals and "superstar portfolio" trackers after the price has already moved. Stop using margin or loans against shares, which is how drawdowns become ruin. Stop treating FII selling as stock-specific news. Stop judging anyone, yourself included, on a one-to-three-year record. Stop buying fading businesses because they look cheap: that was Buffett's own repeated mistake. Stop trading in and out of good funds after bad quarters, since the behavior gap of 1–5 points a year is larger than most picking edges. And stop holding a collapsing stock out of hope when you cannot explain why the business is unharmed. Jhunjhunwala's test of "no permanent impairment of value" is the question to ask, and if the honest answer is "I don't know," the position is too big.

data.section: What this means for you

title: What separated real market winners › What this means for you

body: Institutions have structural advantages in research scale, data, cost, speed and risk systems. In India's F&O market those advantages are decisive and retail cannot copy them. In long-only investing the edges are weaker. Size, benchmark constraints and career risk handicap large managers, and most active funds trail their index over long periods. Retail's real edges are small or illiquid stocks, long holding horizons, no benchmark and no redemption pressure.

data.section: Takeaway

title: fii_prop_firms › Takeaway

body:
**Where wealth comes from**
- Kaplan & Rauh (AER 2013, "Family, Education, and Sources of Wealth among the Richest Americans, 1982–2012"): 69% of the 2011 Forbes 400 started their own business, up from 40% in 1982. The authors credit early access to education, applied in scalable industries (technology, finance, mass retail). — [Stanford GSB](https://www.gsb.stanford.edu/insights/joshua-rauh-what-forbes-400-list-says-about-american-wealth); [Chicago Booth Review](https://www.chicagobooth.edu/review/billionaires-self-made); [RePEc](https://econpapers.repec.org/RePEc:aea:aecrev:v:103:y:2013:i:3:p:158-62)
- Forbes' own self-made score put 70.5% of the 2021 Forbes 400 as self-made, but many of those "self-made" people grew up with advantages. — [Chicago Booth Review](https://www.chicagobooth.edu/review/billionaires-self-made)
- Korom, Lutter & Beckert (Max Planck): self-made entrepreneurs in lucrative fields, *e.g., hedge fund managers*, increasingly populate the Forbes 400. Heirs are *more* likely than self-made entrepreneurs to stay on the list, all else equal. This is a survivorship point: inherited, diversified wealth lasts longer than concentrated founder wealth. — [MPIfG paper](https://pure.mpg.de/pubman/item/item_2418682_8/component/file_2632377/SSR_65_2017_Korom.pdf)
- 2026 Forbes billionaires: about 3,428 billionaires, about 65% self-made (vs about 58% in 2010). "Finance & Investments" was reportedly the largest category, with about 74% of finance billionaires self-made. These numbers come from secondary aggregators, and their definitions of "self-made" differ. — [BusinessStats](https://businesstats.com/?p=5511); [247WallSt (only ~8% fully inherited)](https://247wallst.com/personal-finance/2026/09/15/only-8-of-billionaires-fully-inherited-their-money-heres-how-the-rest-got-rich/)
- Bessembinder: about 4% of U.S. listed stocks since 1926 (about 1,092 of about 26,000) account for *all* net wealth creation over T-bills. Five firms account for 11.9% of it. The majority of stocks underperform T-bills over their lifetimes. — [ASU W.P. Carey](https://blogs.wpcarey.asu.edu/20180917-do-stocks-outperform-treasury-bills); [ASU 2024 update](https://blogs.wpcarey.asu.edu/20240805-asu-study-stock-market-winners-uncovers-some-surprises). A 2026 Strathclyde paper calls the figure replicable but says the interpretation is open to debate: should investors hunt for the 4% or own everything? — [Strathclyde](https://strathprints.strath.ac.uk/97040/1/OConnell-etal-2026-What-does-shareholder-wealth-creation-tell.pdf)

body:
`case_study:nikola-2020` | 2020-09-10 | tickers: US-NKLAQ | confidence: verified

Nikola listed via SPAC (VectoIQ) in Jun 2020 and within days reached an intraday ~$94 (~$30 bn market cap, above Ford) with essentially no revenue. On 10 Sep 2020 Hindenburg's 'Ocean of Lies' report showed, among other things, that the 2018 'Nikola One in motion' video was a truck rolling downhill, and that claimed in-house components were bought from suppliers. Founder Trevor Milton resigned on 20 Sep; the GM partnership was scaled back; Milton was convicted of securities and wire fraud (Oct 2022) and sentenced to 4 years (Dec 2023) -- later pardoned (2025). Nikola filed Chapter 11 in Feb 2025 after burning billions; equity ~0 (after a 1:30 reverse split in 2024). Visible flags: (1) pre-revenue company valued above incumbents; (2) founder making unverifiable technical claims on social media/podcasts; (3) SPAC structure with limited diligence and insider/sponsor lock-up expiries; (4) partnerships announced as validation (GM, CNH/Iveco) with equity-for-tech structures; (5) Hindenburg's work was checkable from public sources and ex-employees. Lesson: SPAC-era pre-revenue stories have terrible base rates; founder credibility can be tested with scuttlebutt; a single falsified claim usually means more.

**Lesson:** Pre-revenue SPAC + promotional founder = avoid
**Spotted early by:** Hindenburg Research
**Links:** illustrates -> `insight:short-seller-reports-outcomes`, illustrates -> `strategy:fisher-scuttlebutt`

body:
- **Explanations come when asked.** Misses are usually explained (Rajasthan monsoon, ROW and transformer/HVDC shortages, CEA holding back bids, the Middle East war, freight, resin prices). But in 28 of 32 shortfalls the explanation came only after an analyst raised it.
- **The exceptions:**
  - the Q1FY27 opening admitted "a lower-than-expected order inflow" for FY26;
  - the polymer headwinds (JJM, resin) were volunteered;
  - the equity raise was explained in the opening remarks;
  - the Oct-26 call warned that margin expansion "will not be as high as what we had targeted". This was pre-emptive and is the most candid moment in the ten calls.
- **Missed numbers get relabelled.** A missed number becomes an "aspiration" afterwards ("25% ... was our aspirational growth"). A lowered number is called "maintaining" ("we maintain ... INR 7,500 crores", when the previous call said 7,000+; exports went from ~1,100 to 1,500).
- **Tone is uniformly high-confidence.** Phrases like "absolutely", "for sure", "well on track", "no challenge" and "no reason for concern" appear whatever the outcome. The closing paragraph has been word-for-word identical boilerplate since Q3FY26 ("growth, profitability and return ratios are set to compound together"). With a weighted delivery ratio of ~41%, this is the **high-tone / middling-delivery mismatch** that the India evidence says retail investors over-reward.
- **Precise, volunteered promises do worst.** By specificity, precise promises delivered 33%, ranges 53% and vague 64%. Volunteered promises delivered 39%, about the same as prompted ones at 42%.
- **Credibility is getting worse.** Promises made in FY25 calls (strong demand, spare capacity) delivered 56%. Promises made in FY26 calls delivered 25%. As growth slowed, the guidance did not adjust fast enough.

**How to use this.**
- Haircut management's dates by 1-2 quarters.
- Haircut segment and new-business targets (polymer, infra, exports, substation) by about half.
- Take group-level margin and finance-cost guidance closer to face value.
- Don't read the tone as information.

| Flag (metric, value, years) | Context questions | Clearing evidence (external) | Confirming evidence | Verdict | What changes my mind | Review date |

| e.g. P/E 95 (TTM), own 10y median 55 | EPS depressed? reverse-DCF growth vs reinvestment x ROIC? | unit data (stores/subs/volumes) supports implied growth | P/E >2x own median; unit growth slowing | open | 2 quarters of unit growth <15% | next results |

Non-overridable: fraud signals, an auditor exit that cites denied information, related-party diversion, and fake-cash signals. A flag cleared only by management's explanation stays **open**. If three or more flags are open, take no position without a variant view.

data.section: Flag override worksheet (copy per candidate)

title: flags_judgment › Flag override worksheet (copy per candidate)

body:
| # | Layer | Question it answers | Time share | Stop when |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| L1 | **Map**: business model, segments, history, peers | What is the unit, and who else runs the same unit? | 5% | You can draw the value chain and name 2–3 peers with comparable units |
| L2 | **Reported financials, re-derived** | Do the numbers add up after accounting adjustments? | 15% | 10-year P&L, BS and CF re-derived; leases, goodwill, ESOP, one-offs separated |
| L3 | **Unit economics** | What does one unit earn, cost and return? | 20% | Revenue per unit and per sq ft or capacity; unit P&L; capex per unit; payback, triangulated two ways |
| L4 | **Line-by-line cost drivers in physical terms** | What *physically* drives each cost, and what is the elasticity to an external input? | 20% | Each cost line ≥3% of sales mapped to quantity × price, with a sensitivity |
| L5 | **Governance, ownership, incentives, related parties** | Who gets paid before minority shareholders? | 10% | RPT table by year and share of each cost line; promoter/PE supply; KMP incentives and strike prices |
| L6 | **Customer, competitor, supplier ground truth** | Does reality match the disclosures? | 20% | Scuttlebutt list executed or scheduled; each observation tied to a model number |
| L7 | **Flag override and synthesis** | Which numbers mislead, in either direction? | 10% | Override table filled; open-flag count; "what would change my mind" per flag |

For a 1-day screen, do L1–L2 plus the L4 top-3 costs plus the L5 RPT table only. **L5's RPT table is never skipped.**

data.section: L13 (2026-11-21) — Depth lives in the boring filings

title: lessons › L13 (2026-11-21) — Depth lives in the boring filings

body:
- **Lakonishok & Lee (2001)**: purchases informative, sales not, effect concentrated in small firms (1975–1995).
  Our data: no detectable effect in $300M–$10B; the $300M–$1B half is the only size slice with a positive
  mean, CI includes zero. Consistent with "small firms drive it" *and* with the effect being largely in
  micro-caps (< $300M), which our filter excluded on purpose (liquidity).
- **Cohen, Malloy & Pomorski (2012)**: ~82 bp/month (~10%/yr) value-weighted for *opportunistic* insiders,
  ~0 for routine ones (1986–2007). We did **not** apply the routine/opportunistic split (needs 3 prior years of each
  insider's history). Our 12m CI upper bound (+5.0%, or ≈ +7% with a generous survivorship add-on) is below
  ~10%/yr, so a naive "any cluster" rule does not capture a CMP-sized edge in 2021–2024. Possible reasons:
  dilution by routine buyers; decay after publication (signal is free and widely screened — OpenInsider,
  Form 4 bots); period-specific regime (mega-cap leadership, 2022 rate shock, regional-bank stress in 2023).

| **Lender (bank / NBFC; v1.3, see the adaptation section)** | **(1) Branch** (deposits, CASA, sourcing per outlet), **(2) loan segment/cohort** (yield, slippage, LGD), **(3) liability pool** (CASA, retail TD, NRI/FCNR, bulk), **(4) balance-sheet "cost lines"** (CRR, PSL shortfall, DICGC) | IBA wage settlement, deposit repricing lag vs EBLR share, DICGC premium, CRR/PSL rules, special funding windows, write-offs vs slippage, collateral price (gold LTV) |
| Platform / software | Cohort / account | CAC, retention, take rate |
| **US widely held company (v1.2)** | Same unit as its business type, plus **management as the "related party"** | KPI definitions (payback, comps, "adjusted"), SBC and retention awards, 8-K Item 5.02 pay and perks, Form 4 clusters, guidance-beat pattern |

title: lessons › L13 (2026-11-21) — Depth lives in the boring filings

body:
The rule is the one fixed in `AUTO_COMPONENTS_peer_comparison.md` section 5, coded in `scripts_auto_peers/make_seed.py`. `scripts_it_peers/make_seed.py` is a copy with the same constants: MIN_N = 5, MIN_POOL = 8, MIN_PEERS = 2, SHRINK_K = 20. It writes the same `adjustment_rule` string to `it_summary.json`. It ran before `make_calls.py` wrote any call, and no probability was typed by hand.

1. Category: revenue_growth, margin, capacity, or other. The new IT categories deal_wins, people and client_concentration map to "other".
2. P(base) = p0 = leave-one-out pooled **strict** delivery of the other three peers in that category, specificity-weighted. If the peers have fewer than 8 scored promises in the category, the all-category peer rate is used. In IT this falls back for margin and other at most companies (peer n = 3–8), and for revenue at Mphasis.
3. SAC_i on the credit basis. Categories with n < 5 or fewer than 2 peers are pooled.
4. P(ours) = clip(p0 + N/(N+20) × SAC/100, 0.05, 0.95).
5. No other adjustment. In-year progress is ignored on purpose (KPIT H1 EBITDA, Coforge H1 EBIT).
6. Scoring: Brier(ours) vs Brier(base), for this batch and pooled with the 16 auto-components calls.

The only code change was a `None` guard: IT has no capacity promises, so the capacity median is empty. It does not change any number for a category that has data.
